Co-lending: two balance sheets, one loan

After this lesson you can:
  • Explain the co-lending model and its funding mechanics
  • State the share, retention, blended-rate and escrow rules
  • Describe loan-level allocation and partner reconciliation

Learning rhythm: read one section at a time, pause to explain the control in your own words, then answer the knowledge check without looking back.

On this page
  1. Why two lenders share one loan
  2. One borrower, two ledgers
  3. Adjacent structures
  4. Regulatory anchors
  5. Where this lives in LoanOS
  6. Knowledge check

1. Why two lenders share one loan

Co-lending pairs complementary strengths: typically an NBFC's origination reach and a bank's cheap capital, jointly funding loans under a prior master agreement. The borrower gets credit that neither partner would extend alone; each partner books its share.

The 2025 arrangements rulebook: funding shares are disclosed and sum to 100%; the originating RE retains a minimum share (a retention floor — skin in the game, no originate-and-dump); the borrower sees one blended rate (the weighted price of both partners' funds — not two confusing rates); and all money moves through an escrow account — no routing through a single partner's books that could disguise the arrangement.

2. One borrower, two ledgers

Operationally, every rupee event splits by share: disbursement funds arrive from both partners via escrow; each EMI's principal, interest and charges allocate loan-level to each partner's ledger legs; fees and taxes divide per agreement; collections and recoveries (including from module 6's paths) allocate by share. Partner reconciliation runs on statements and break management like any other financial interface.

Servicing stays single-faced: the borrower deals with one servicer, one grievance path, one KFS — the co-lending complexity is the lenders' problem, never the borrower's. LoanOS's co-lending module implements the agreement, share validation, blended-rate math and escrow routing.

3. Adjacent structures

A BA should recognise the neighbours: direct assignment / portfolio sale (transferring existing loans), securitisation (pooling and tranching), servicing transfer (moving the servicing duty), and participation. Each has its own rulebook; the platform's transfer capabilities model them separately from co-lending, which is a *joint origination* structure, not a transfer.

Regulatory anchors

  • RBI-CLA-2025 — Co-lending: prior agreement, disclosed shares summing to 100%, retention floor, single blended rate, escrow routing.
  • RBI-FUND-FLOW — Escrow is the permitted exception to direct flow — single-partner pass-through remains prohibited.

Family IDs resolve in the India regulatory register (docs/compliance/india-regulatory-register.md), which owns sources and caveats.

Retrieval practice

Knowledge check

Answer aloud or write your choice before opening the explanation. If you miss it, revisit the named section—not the whole lesson.

1. In an 80/20 bank/NBFC co-lending pact, the borrower's rate is…

  1. The bank's rate on 80% and the NBFC's on 20%, shown separately
  2. One blended rate weighted across both partners' pricing
  3. The higher of the two
  4. Negotiable per EMI
Reveal answer and reasoning

B. The borrower sees a single all-in blended rate; the internal split is the partners' accounting, not the borrower's problem.

2. Why must co-lending funds move through escrow?

  1. Faster settlement
  2. So neither partner's account becomes an undisclosed pass-through controlling the joint flows
  3. Tax efficiency
  4. RBI charges fees on escrow
Reveal answer and reasoning

B. Escrow keeps the joint funding transparent and prevents single-partner control — the co-lending-specific application of the fund-flow principle.
